textbookText: Figure: 9.2.2 Reflex arc Reflex arc is formed by following components: a. Receptor organs: They are sensory organs like skin eye ear tongue etc. which receive stimuli. These organs have nerve endings which generate sensory impulses after the perception of specific stimulus. b. Sensory or afferent nerves: Those nerves which transmit impulses or informations from sensory organ to brain and spinal cord are called sensory nerves. Cell body of afferent nerve lies inside the dorsal root of spinal cord. c. Motor or efferent nerves: Those nerves which conduct motor impulses from brain and spinal cord to effector organs are called motor nerves. Cell body of efferent nerve lies inside the ventral root of spinal cord. d. Modulator: It is the central nervous system (brain and spinal cord) which modifies sensory impulses to motor impulses. Inside the spinal cord, grey mater contains interneuron which forms synapse (nerves junction) with both sensory nerve and motor nerves. Interneurons act as the bridge for incoming and outgoing impulses. In some reflexes (monosynaptic reflex), there may not be interneuron where impulses are directly passed from sensory neuron to motor neuron through synapse. e. Effector organs: Those organs which respond to stimuli or external environmental factors are called effector organ. Effector organs are muscles and glands.

Mechanism of reflex action: The receptor organs are innervated by sensory nerve endings. Such nerve endings induce sensory impulses or information after detecting stimulus, which pass through sensory neuron and reach spinal cord or brain where information is processed and transformed into motor impulses and then such impulses transmit through motor nerve to reach effector organs. Four sequential steps of reflex action consist of reception, conduction, modulation (interpretation) and effect.

Example: In the case of touching cold object or ice, receptors in finger detect stimulus (ice) resulting the production of impulses. Such impulses are transmitted to spinal cord through sensory nerves. In spinal cord, sensory impulses are modified as motor impulses which are Biology, Grade 11 | 445
transmitted through motor neuron to the arm muscles. Now, these muscles contract quickly and hand is pulled away.
Significance of reflex action i. Reflex action prevents overloading of brain because spinal cord is also involved in this process. ii. Reflex action protects animals from harmful stimuli.
9.2.3 TAXES
Questions to think? An earthworm when kept in a brighter place starts crawling towards dark. Why?

In general, animals adjust their body posture in normal or balanced position in space. If animals are exposed to some environmental factors or stimuli, they orient their body either towards stimuli or move away from these stimuli. Such a directional movement of organisms in response to external stimulus is called is called a taxis. When the organism or cell moves towards the source of stimulation, it is called positive taxis. If the organism or cell moves away from the source of stimulation it is called negative taxis. Taxis can also be defined as the behavioural response of an organism to external stimuli.
Examples: Bacteria are attracted towards nutrient such as sugar amino acid (attraction or positive response) but repelled by harmful substances and bacterial wastes (repulsion or negative response).
Euglena avoids salt solution (repulsion or negative response) but attracted towards glucose solution (attraction or positive response)
Cock roaches discard lighted area (repulsion or negative response).
TYPES OF TAXES
On the basis of type or nature of stimulus perceived by animals

1. Phototaxis: Phototaxis is defined as the movement of animals either towards light or escape away from light. Example: Earthworm, mosquito, cockroach etc. move away from bright light showing negative phototaxis but Euglena, moth, housefly etc. move towards lighted area showing positive phototaxis. 2. Chemotaxis: Chemotaxis is defined as the movement of organism either towards a chemical stimulus or away from it. Example: Euglena moves away from strong acid (negative chemotaxis) but moves towards weak acid solution (positive chemotaxis).

Figure: 9.2.4 Mosquito flying away from mosquito repellant 3. Thermotaxis: Directional movement of organism in response to temperature is called thermotaxis. Paramecium prefers to live in water of temperature ranging from 24°c 28°c but avoids below 24°c or above 28°c. Hydra prefers to live in cold water but escapes away if water temperature exceeds 25°c. 4. Thigmotaxis: It is the response of an organism to physical contact or touch stimulus. Paramecium and Amoeba move away (negative thigmotaxis) from an object after touching it. Earwigs seek contact with a solid object showing positive thigmotaxis.
